implementation_notes: RSpec's doubles are first-class objects: double('warehouse') is a loose double, instance_double(Warehouse) verifies method names and arity against the real class, allow(obj).to receive(:method).and_return(value) stubs behaviour, and expect(obj).to receive(:method).with(args).once sets a message expectation that fails the example at teardown if unmet. Expectations are configured per message rather than per object, ordering is opt-in with .ordered, and verification is automatic - there is no explicit verify call, which removes the final-verification trap but also means a loose double's missing interface check surfaces only when the message is stubbed or received.
code_sketch:
warehouse = instance_double(Warehouse)
allow(warehouse).to receive(:has_inventory).with("Talisker", 50).and_return(true)
expect(warehouse).to receive(:remove).with("Talisker", 50).once

order = Order.new("Talisker", 50)
expect(order.fill(warehouse)).to be(true)
pitfalls: Loose doubles accept any message and complain about none of them, so interface drift goes unnoticed; use instance_double/class_double so every stub must match a real method.

Message expectations are verified at example teardown, so failures surface far from the interaction - and stubs created with allow() are never verified at all, so a call that should have happened can go unchecked.
Call order is accepted by default; add .ordered (or an ordered group) only where the protocol really requires it, because it makes the example order-sensitive.
